claim: The bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST) has been implicated in conditioned fear and anxiety.
source: The bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST) has been implicated in conditioned fear and anxiety, but the specific factors that engage the BNST in defensive behaviors are unclear.
evidence: This is a general statement about prior research on the BNST, supported by the broader scientific literature.

claim: The specific factors that engage the BNST in defensive behaviors are unclear.

evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that motivates the current study.

claim: Reversible inactivation of the BNST selectively reduced freezing to CSs that poorly signaled US onset (e.g., a backward CS that followed the US).
source: Reversible inactivation of the BNST selectively reduced freezing to CSs that poorly signaled US onset (e.g., a backward CS that followed the US), but did not eliminate freezing to forward CSs even when they predicted USs of variable intensity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the inactivation experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: Reversible inactivation of the BNST did not eliminate freezing to forward CSs even when they predicted USs of variable intensity.
source: Reversible inactivation of the BNST selectively reduced freezing to CSs that poorly signaled US onset (e.g., a backward CS that followed the US), but did not eliminate freezing to forward CSs even when they predicted USs of variable intensity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the variable intensity experiment.

claim: Backward (but not forward) CSs selectively increased Fos in the ventral BNST.
source: Additionally, backward (but not forward) CSs selectively increased Fos in the ventral BNST and in BNST-projecting neurons in the infralimbic region of the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), but not in the hippocampus or amygdala.
evidence: This claim is supported by Fos immunohistochemistry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Backward (but not forward) CSs selectively increased Fos in BNST-projecting neurons in the infralimbic region of the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC).
source: Additionally, backward (but not forward) CSs selectively increased Fos in the ventral BNST and in BNST-projecting neurons in the infralimbic region of the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), but not in the hippocampus or amygdala.
evidence: This claim is supported by Fos-CTb double-labeling data.

claim: Backward CSs did not selectively increase Fos in the hippocampus or amygdala.
source: Additionally, backward (but not forward) CSs selectively increased Fos in the ventral BNST and in BNST-projecting neurons in the infralimbic region of the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), but not in the hippocampus or amygdala.
evidence: This claim is supported by Fos immunohistochemistry data showing no selective increase in these regions.

claim: BNST circuits regulate fear to unpredictable threats.
source: These data reveal that BNST circuits regulate fear to unpredictable threats, which may be critical to the etiology and expression of anxiety.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: BNST regulation of fear to unpredictable threats may be critical to the etiology and expression of anxiety.
source: These data reveal that BNST circuits regulate fear to unpredictable threats, which may be critical to the etiology and expression of anxiety.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: Excessive apprehension about potential future threats is a defining feature of many anxiety disorders, including generalized anxiety disorder (GAD).
source: Excessive apprehension about potential future threats, including financial loss, illness, or death, is a defining feature of many anxiety disorders, including generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) (Behar et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Anxiety and trauma-related disorders are widespread and costly.
source: Anxiety and trauma-related disorders are widespread and costly (Blanco et al., 2011; Comer et al., 2011; Kinley et al., 2011; Salas-Wright et al., 2014; Stein et al., 2017; Wittchen, 2002), and remain difficult to treat (Colvonen et al., 2017; Costello et al., 2014; Iza et al., 2013; Sinnema et al., 2015).

claim: Anxiety and trauma-related disorders remain difficult to treat.
source: Anxiety and trauma-related disorders are widespread and costly (Blanco et al., 2011; Comer et al., 2011; Kinley et al., 2011; Salas-Wright et al., 2014; Stein et al., 2017; Wittchen, 2002), and remain difficult to treat (Colvonen et al., 2017; Costello et al., 2014; Iza et al., 2013; Sinnema et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Understanding the neural circuits underlying anxiety is important for refining behavioral and pharmacotherapeutic treatments.
source: Understanding the neural circuits underlying anxiety is important for refining behavioral and pharmacotherapeutic treatments (Berridge, 2018; Deslauriers et al., 2018; Fanselow and Pennington, 2018; Fanselow and Pennington, 2017; Graham et al., 2014; LeDoux and Daw, 2018; Nees et al., 2015; Pine and LeDoux, 2017; Tye, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

source: Several recent studies have demonstrated changes in the function of the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST) in individuals with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and anxiety disorders (Andreescu et al., 2015; Brinkmann et al., 2018; Brinkmann et al., 2017b; Brinkmann et al., 2017a; Buff et al., 2017; Münsterkötter et al., 2015; Rabellino et al., 2018; Straube et al., 2007; Yassa et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The conditions that recruit the BNST to aversive learning and memory processes believed to underlie anxiety disorders are still not understood.
source: However, the conditions that recruit the BNST to aversive learning and memory processes believed to underlie anxiety disorders are still not understood (Avery et al., 2016; Avery et al., 2014; Ch'ng et al., 2018; Daniel and Rainnie, 2016; Davis et al., 2010; Fox and Shackman, 2019; Goode and Maren, 2017; Gungor and Paré, 2016; Lebow and Chen, 2016; Perusini and Fanselow, 2015; Shackman and Fox, 2016; Walker et al., 2009; Walker and Davis, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature and identifies a gap in knowledge.

claim: BNST lesions in rats impair defensive behaviors evoked by unconditioned threats.
source: Early work on this question revealed that BNST lesions in rats impair defensive behaviors evoked by unconditioned threats (Gewirtz et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: BNST inactivation results in a loss of unconditioned defensive responding to the presence of predator odors.
source: For example, BNST inactivation results in a loss of unconditioned defensive responding to the presence of predator odors (Breitfeld et al., 2015; Fendt et al., 2003; Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Unconditioned increases in the acoustic startle reflex produced by either intracranial administration of corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF) or exposure to bright light require the BNST.
source: Additionally, unconditioned increases in the acoustic startle reflex produced by either intracranial administration of corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF) or exposure to bright light require the BNST, whereas fear-potentiated startle to punctate conditioned stimuli (CSs) do not (Walker et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Fear-potentiated startle to punctate conditioned stimuli (CSs) does not require the BNST.
source: Additionally, unconditioned increases in the acoustic startle reflex produced by either intracranial administration of corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF) or exposure to bright light require the BNST, whereas fear-potentiated startle to punctate conditioned stimuli (CSs) do not (Walker et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: BNST lesions produce deficits in both freezing and corticosterone release elicited by contextual, but not auditory, CSs after Pavlovian fear conditioning in rats.
source: However, the involvement of the BNST in defensive responding is not restricted to unconditioned threat: BNST lesions produce deficits in both freezing and corticosterone release elicited by contextual, but not auditory, CSs after Pavlovian fear conditioning in rats (LeDoux et al., 1988; Sullivan et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: It is not stimulus modality that differentiates the effects of BNST lesions on tone and context freezing.
source: Interestingly, however, it is not stimulus modality that differentiates the effects of BNST lesions on tone and context freezing.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from prior research findings.

claim: BNST lesions impair freezing responses to long-duration (e.g., 10 min) auditory conditioned stimuli (CSs).
source: BNST lesions impair freezing responses to long-duration (e.g., 10 min) auditory conditioned stimuli (CSs) (Waddell et al., 2006), and spare freezing to short-duration (1 min) contextual stimuli (Hammack et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: BNST lesions spare freezing to short-duration (1 min) contextual stimuli.
source: BNST lesions impair freezing responses to long-duration (e.g., 10 min) auditory conditioned stimuli (CSs) (Waddell et al., 2006), and spare freezing to short-duration (1 min) contextual stimuli (Hammack et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: It has been proposed that the BNST is required to organize behavioral and hormonal responses to sustained threats (whether conditioned or unconditioned).
source: Based on this work, it has been proposed that the BNST is required to organize behavioral and hormonal responses to sustained threats (whether conditioned or unconditioned) (Hammack et al., 2015; Hammack et al., 2009; Takahashi, 2014; Waddell et al., 2008; Waddell et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The duration of the behavioral responses is confounded with the duration of the eliciting stimulus.
source: Of course, the duration of the behavioral responses in these situations is confounded with the duration of the eliciting stimulus.
evidence: This is an inference about the interpretation of prior research.

claim: The BNST mediates sustained defensive responses independent of the specific features and durations of the stimuli that evoke them.
source: Thus, it has been argued that the BNST mediates sustained defensive responses independent of the specific features and durations of the stimuli that evoke them (Davis, 2006; Davis et al., 2010; Walker et al., 2009; Walker and Davis, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Long-duration CSs or contexts provide relatively poor information about when a future unconditioned stimulus (US) will occur.
source: For example, long-duration CSs or contexts provide relatively poor information about when a future unconditioned stimulus (US) will occur (i.e., the US will occur at some distal time in the future), whereas short-duration CSs or contexts provide more immediate certainty about the temporal imminence of US onset (i.e., the US will occur soon).
evidence: This is an inference about the temporal information provided by different types of stimuli.

claim: Short-duration CSs or contexts provide more immediate certainty about the temporal imminence of US onset.
source: For example, long-duration CSs or contexts provide relatively poor information about when a future unconditioned stimulus (US) will occur (i.e., the US will occur at some distal time in the future), whereas short-duration CSs or contexts provide more immediate certainty about the temporal imminence of US onset (i.e., the US will occur soon).
evidence: This is an inference about the temporal information provided by different types of stimuli.

claim: The BNST may have a critical role in processing temporally unpredictable threats.
source: We and others have proposed that the BNST may have a critical role in processing temporally unpredictable threats, particularly in mediating defensive responses to threatening stimuli that poorly predict when an aversive event will occur (Goode and Maren, 2017; Lange et al., 2017; Luyck et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Punctate auditory CSs that are followed by shock at unpredictable latencies yield freezing responses that are sensitive to BNST manipulations.
source: Consistent with this view, punctate auditory CSs that are followed by shock at unpredictable latencies yield freezing responses that are sensitive to BNST manipulations (Daldrup et al., 2016; Lange et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A crucial parameter that determines the role for the BNST in defensive behavior is the information a signal provides about when an aversive event will occur.
source: This suggests that a crucial parameter that determines the role for the BNST in defensive behavior is neither the duration nor modality of the threat (nor the duration of the elicited defensive response), but rather the information a signal provides about when an aversive event will occur.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from prior research findings.

claim: Extensively-trained BW CSs become conditioned inhibitors that dampen responding to other first-order excitatory cues.
source: Although extensively-trained BW CSs become conditioned inhibitors that dampen responding to other first-order excitatory cues (Andreatta et al., 2012; Ayres et al., 1976; Christianson et al., 2011; Gerber et al., 2014; Moscovitch and LoLordo, 1968; Siegel and Domjan, 1971), minimally-trained BW CSs elicit excitatory conditioned responses that transfer across contexts (Ayres et al., 1987; Barnet and Miller, 1996; Bevins and Ayres, 1992; Chang et al., 2003; Connor et al., 2017; Heth, 1976; Mahoney and Ayres, 1976; Prével et al., 2018; Prével et al., 2016; Rescorla, 1968).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Minimally-trained BW CSs elicit excitatory conditioned responses that transfer across contexts.
source: Although extensively-trained BW CSs become conditioned inhibitors that dampen responding to other first-order excitatory cues (Andreatta et al., 2012; Ayres et al., 1976; Christianson et al., 2011; Gerber et al., 2014; Moscovitch and LoLordo, 1968; Siegel and Domjan, 1971), minimally-trained BW CSs elicit excitatory conditioned responses that transfer across contexts (Ayres et al., 1987; Barnet and Miller, 1996; Bevins and Ayres, 1992; Chang et al., 2003; Connor et al., 2017; Heth, 1976; Mahoney and Ayres, 1976; Prével et al., 2018; Prével et al., 2016; Rescorla, 1968).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: BNST inactivation reduced freezing to a BW, but not FW, CS.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, we found that BNST inactivation reduced freezing to a BW, but not FW, CS.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the inactivation experiments.

claim: The effect of BNST inactivation on BW CS freezing was related to the uncertainty of the BW CS in predicting US onset.
source: This effect was related to the uncertainty of the BW CS in predicting US onset, because the same outcome was observed when USs occurred randomly with respect to the CS.
evidence: This is an inference supported by experimental data from the random US experiment.

claim: Freezing to the backward CS was less sustained than that to the forward CS.
source: Interestingly, freezing to the backward CS was less sustained than that to the forward CS, suggesting that neither long-duration stimuli nor sustained freezing responses are required to recruit the BNST.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the behavioral tests.

claim: Neither long-duration stimuli nor sustained freezing responses are required to recruit the BNST.
source: Interestingly, freezing to the backward CS was less sustained than that to the forward CS, suggesting that neither long-duration stimuli nor sustained freezing responses are required to recruit the BNST.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Both forward and backward CSs increased Fos expression in the hippocampus, BNST, amygdala, and mPFC.
source: Finally, although both forward and backward CSs increased Fos expression in the hippocampus, BNST, amygdala, and mPFC, only backward CSs selectively increased Fos expression in both the ventral BNST and BNST-projecting neurons in the infralimbic cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by Fos immunohistochemistry data.

claim: Only backward CSs selectively increased Fos expression in both the ventral BNST and BNST-projecting neurons in the infralimbic cortex.
source: Finally, although both forward and backward CSs increased Fos expression in the hippocampus, BNST, amygdala, and mPFC, only backward CSs selectively increased Fos expression in both the ventral BNST and BNST-projecting neurons in the infralimbic cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by Fos immunohistochemistry and Fos-CTb double-labeling data.

claim: The BNST and its mPFC afferents may mediate defensive responding to threats that signal uncertain or remote onset of shock.
source: Collectively, these data reveal that the BNST and its mPFC afferents may mediate defensive responding to threats that signal uncertain or remote onset of shock.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Unpredictable threats come in many forms including uncertain timing, magnitude or type, or probability of threat.
source: Unpredictable threats come in many forms [including uncertain timing, magnitude or type, or probability of threat: (Bennett et al., 2018; Daldrup et al., 2015; Davies and Craske, 2015; McHugh et al., 2015; McNally et al., 2011; Schroijen et al., 2016; Seidenbecher et al., 2016); these subtypes of uncertainty may have dissociable and cumulative contributions to anxiety.

claim: Subtypes of uncertainty may have dissociable and cumulative contributions to anxiety.
source: Unpredictable threats come in many forms [including uncertain timing, magnitude or type, or probability of threat: (Bennett et al., 2018; Daldrup et al., 2015; Davies and Craske, 2015; McHugh et al., 2015; McNally et al., 2011; Schroijen et al., 2016; Seidenbecher et al., 2016); these subtypes of uncertainty may have dissociable and cumulative contributions to anxiety.

source: In particular, uncertainty about the timing of the onset of aversive events has been linked to measures of anxiety in humans and other animals (Amadi et al., 2017; Bennett et al., 2018; Shankman et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Unpredictable threats are associated with increases or changes in regional cerebral blood flow and functional connectivity in the primate BNST.
source: Interestingly, unpredictable threats (of varying types and degrees) are associated with increases or changes in regional cerebral blood flow and functional connectivity in the primate BNST (Alvarez et al., 2015; Alvarez et al., 2011; Brinkmann et al., 2018; Brinkmann et al., 2017a; Brinkmann et al., 2017b; Buff et al., 2017; Choi et al., 2014; Choi et al., 2012; Coaster et al., 2011; Fox et al., 2018; Grupe et al., 2013; Herrmann et al., 2016; Kalin et al., 2008; Kalin et al., 2005; Klumpers et al., 2017; Klumpers et al., 2015; McMenamin et al., 2014; Meyer et al., 2019; Mobbs et al., 2010; Münsterkötter et al., 2015; Naaz et al., 2019; Pedersen et al., 2018; Pedersen et al., 2017; Schlund et al., 2013; Sladky et al., 2018; Somerville et al., 2010; Torrisi et al., 2018).

source: However, we and others have shown that BNST lesions or inactivation reduce the expression of freezing even when those levels are relatively high (Goode et al., 2015; Hammack et al., 2015).

source: Hence, the BNST mediates fear to cues that signal uncertain or remote threat, independent of the duration of the antecedent stimuli or behavioral responses associated with the threat (Goode and Maren, 2017).

evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

source: Increases in immediate early gene expression, metabolic activity, and changes in electrophysiological firing patterns have been observed in the BNST in response to direct exposure to conditioned contextual cues (Campeau et al., 1997; Daldrup et al., 2016; Jennings et al., 2013; Lemos et al., 2010; Luyten et al., 2012; Marcinkiewcz et al., 2016).

source: If the backward CS functions similarly to a conditioned context, then one might expect Fos activity to be elevated in the BNST of animals exposed to the backward CS.

source: There is growing evidence for a regulatory role for prefrontal connections to the BNST in stress and anxiety-like behavior (Fox et al., 2010; Glangetas et al., 2017; Glangetas et al., 2013; Johnson et al., 2019; Kinnison et al., 2012; Motzkin et al., 2015; Naaz et al., 2019; Radley et al., 2009), the present data adds to this work by suggesting that the IL may be involved in generating freezing and/or stress responding to the backward CS.

evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the shock reactivity data.

source: All animals exhibited a reliable decrease in shock-induced activity across the conditioning session (repeated measures: F5,150 = 9.59, p < 0.0001) and the rate of decline in activity was similar in the two groups (no trial × group interaction: F < 1.70, p > 0.09), but the overall level of shock-induced activity was significantly lower in the FW animals (main effect of group: F1,30 = 9.59, p < 0.05; significant two-tailed unpaired t-test for mean levels: t30 = -2.08, p < 0.05).
